Confirmed via ls that _backend-system/ holds only README.md, research/, and audit/ (audit/ has 8 files, no observability.md or reliability.md audit, and no LAW.md/RATIONALE.md/AUDIT_2026-07-16.md/QUESTIONS.md exist at the folder root). Read instrumentation.ts (env-assert only, no tracing/metrics), lib/health.ts (three-probe dependency check), lib/cron-run.ts, lib/error-report.ts, lib/alert-admin.ts, lib/audit.ts, app/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts (full), app/api/cron/reconcile/route.ts (header), app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (lines 1-70+), .github/workflows/cron-jobs.yml and .github/actions/ping-cron/action.yml, _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md (full, 73 lines), _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md (observability TOC line only), netlify.toml. Ran greps across app/ and lib/ for console.* counts (897 total: 276 files in app, 47 in lib), for requestId/traceparent/x-request-id (2 unrelated hits, both a domain field not a tracing id), for pino/winston/bunyan structured loggers (0 hits), for captureException (0 hits), for logAuditEvent call sites (29, all admin-initiated) versus the automatic money-movement files (issue-refund.ts, issue-purchase-refund.ts, release-deposits, release-payments: 0 hits), for alertAdmin call sites (11), for raw email/phone interpolated into console.* calls (1 hit), and for runbook/postmortem/incident files repo-wide (only _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md and mentions inside _backend-system/research/*.md, no postmortem file anywhere). findings.title: Cron-health check detects failed runs, not missing runs
findings.principle: Every cron-health check must distinguish 'ran and failed' from 'never ran.' Maintain an EXPECTED_CRON_NAMES map (name to its scheduled interval) and, in the daily digest (or a dedicated check), assert for each name that a cron_runs row exists within 2x its own interval; treat a missing row as a failure at the same severity as ok:false, not silence. Separately, wire one externally-hosted heartbeat (a free dead-man's-switch service, or an UptimeRobot-style ping) so a fully disabled or silently-broken GitHub Actions scheduler is itself detected, independent of anything running inside GitHub Actions.
findings.why: Absence-of-evidence read as evidence-of-absence is this project's own named #1 failure class (the 'silent no-ops' rule in CLAUDE.md, there applied to DB filters); here it applies to the monitoring system itself. If GitHub Actions ever stops scheduling the workflow (or a YAML edit silently breaks the schedule trigger), zero cron_runs rows get written, and the daily digest's own query for 'ok=false in the last 24h' returns zero, reporting a false 'all clear' on the exact day everything actually stopped. Right-sized now: a query rewrite plus one owner-account signup for the external heartbeat, not a paging platform; revisit a fuller on-call/paging tier only once there is more than one person who could be woken.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts lines 93-118: the only cron-health query is `.from('cron_runs').select(...).eq('ok', false).gte('ran_at', twentyFourHoursAgo)`, which returns nothing (and renders '0 cron failures') if a cron simply never ran. 26 cron routes exist under app/api/cron (`find app/api/cron -name route.ts | wc -l` = 26), all scheduled purely by `.github/workflows/cron-jobs.yml`'s `schedule:` triggers, with no code anywhere checking for the presence of an expected run.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "cron_runs" app lib --include=*.ts across the whole repo returns only the insert in lib/cron-run.ts and the ok=false read in daily-digest/route.ts, no presence/expected-count check. grep -rniE "expected.?run|missing.?run|dead.?man|heartbeat|healthchecks\.io|cronitor" across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _plans, CLAUDE.md, .claude/hooks returned zero hits. GitHub's own docs (verified via WebFetch this session against docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows): 'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days,' confirming this is a real, named GitHub Actions failure mode, not a hypothetical.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: lib/cron-run.ts writes {ok, processed, duration_ms, errors} per run and the ping-cron GH Action hard-asserts ok:true on the HTTP response (catching an error INSIDE a run that DID fire); the every-15-min job also curls /api/health and fails red on a down site. None of this catches the scheduler itself going silent.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (Observability section) for the principle; app/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts for the presence-check query; _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md 'Monitoring' section for the external-heartbeat owner action item.
findings.enforcement: gate:cron-presence-check , a query asserting every name in EXPECTED_CRON_NAMES has a cron_runs row within 2x its interval, wired into the existing daily-digest email; the external heartbeat is an owner one-time signup, not agent-enforceable.

findings.title: Stripe webhook signature and claim failures only console.error, never alert
findings.principle: Every Stripe webhook rejection path -- signature verification failure and the event-claim DB-error branch -- must call reportError(scope, err, context), the same throttled admin-alert path already used for handler-body exceptions later in the same file, instead of a bare console.error. A sustained run of signature failures (a rotated or misconfigured STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET) or claim-insert failures (a broken processed_webhook_events table, the project's own documented past bug class) must reach a human within the existing 15-minute throttle window, not only exist in Netlify's 24-hour-to-7-day function-log window.
findings.why: The org's own research (section 8) already establishes that Netlify function-log retention is 24h-7d and nothing durable exists beyond it. If the webhook secret is ever rotated or misconfigured, every single Stripe event fails signature verification silently forever: customers are charged in Stripe but no booking ever confirms server-side, and the only trace is a console.error line that ages out within a week. This is a money-path blind spot, not a hypothetical: the project already tracks a near-identical rotation risk for Apple's login secret in memory, so secret rotation is a known recurring operational event here.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts lines 34-36 (signature verification catch: `console.error("[stripe/webhook] Signature verification failed:", err); return NextResponse.json(..., { status: 400 })`, no reportError call) and lines 60-63 (claim-insert error branch, non-23505 path: `console.error("[stripe/webhook] failed to claim event:", claimError, ...)`, no reportError call). reportError IS imported and used later in the same file, inside individual event-type case handlers (confirmed by reading the file), so the two earliest and most systemic rejection points are the two left unwired.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "reportError\|alertAdmin" app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts shows reportError used further down the file (inside the switch statement's per-event-type catch blocks) but the sig-verify catch (line 34) and the claim-error branch (line 61) return early before any such call, confirmed by direct read of lines 1-70.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the alert-on-throw infrastructure (reportError, throttled alertAdmin) already exists and is already wired for handler-body exceptions in this exact file; only the two top-level rejection branches are missing the call.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts lines 34-36 and 60-63 (two one-line additions); _backend-system/LAW.md Observability section as a standing rule ('every webhook rejection branch reports, not just handler-body throws').
findings.enforcement: gate:webhook-rejection-alerting , a lint or CI grep that flags any `return NextResponse.json` inside a webhook route's error branch that isn't preceded by a reportError/alertAdmin call in the same block.

findings.title: Audit trail exists but automatic money-movement paths don't write to it
findings.principle: Every function that moves money or changes a payment/payout state without a human clicking a button in the admin UI -- an automatic refund issued from the dispute engine or a webhook handler, a cron-driven payout release, an off-session charge -- writes one audit_log row (via logAuditEvent or a system-actor variant of it) in the SAME code path that performs the mutation, not as a caller's optional responsibility. Enforce this with a CI check: any diff touching lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts, lib/purchases/issue-purchase-refund.ts, app/api/cron/release-deposits/route.ts, app/api/cron/release-payments/route.ts, or lib/bookings/off-session-charge.ts must also touch (or already import) logAuditEvent, or the check fails with a named reason.
findings.why: audit_log is well-built and already used for 29 admin-initiated actions, but the automatic money paths -- exactly the ones a real dispute ('why did my payout change') would need answered months later -- currently have zero rows. lib/bookings/charge-fee.ts even states outright that logging is 'the CALLER's responsibility,' which is an unenforced convention a future session with no memory of this file will not know to honor. Right-sized now: this is a Postgres INSERT into an existing table, not a new audit platform; a dedicated tamper-proof ledger product is genuinely premature until a specific compliance regime (a processor's audit requirement, an FDPIC inquiry) names cryptographic tamper-evidence as a hard requirement.
findings.local_evidence: grep -n logAuditEvent across lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts, lib/purchases/issue-purchase-refund.ts, app/api/cron/release-deposits/route.ts, app/api/cron/release-payments/route.ts, lib/bookings/off-session-charge.ts, lib/bookings/charge-fee.ts returns zero call sites; lib/bookings/charge-fee.ts line 273 states directly: 'Audit (logAuditEvent) is the CALLER's responsibility -- this chokepoint is [not the place].' Meanwhile grep -rl logAuditEvent app lib finds 29 files, all admin-route-initiated (approvals, freezes, disputes, GDPR deletions).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: audit_log table + logAuditEvent helper are fully built (lib/audit.ts) and used for 29 admin-action call sites; zero of the checked automatic money-movement call sites use it.
findings.where_it_should_live: the 5 files named above (add the write inline); _backend-system/LAW.md Observability section as the standing rule; a CI grep gate.
findings.enforcement: gate:money-path-audit-write , CI grep that any diff to the 5 named files also references logAuditEvent (or an explicit documented exemption comment).

findings.title: No request/correlation id anywhere, still unimplemented 10 days after the org's own research named it priority 1
findings.principle: Generate one crypto.randomUUID() per inbound request (in middleware.ts, or a thin withRequestId wrapper at the top of each route handler where middleware doesn't run), thread it through every console.error/console.log call made during that request's lifetime as an explicit first field, and shape the id as a valid W3C traceparent (00-<32 hex>-<16 hex>-01) even though nothing parses it as a real distributed trace yet, so a future tracing backend is a drop-in, not a rewrite. Do this before migrating the log payload itself to full JSON structured logging (that migration is lower priority and can lag file by file).
findings.why: The org's own observability.md (section 1, 'Recommended default for Solen') already named this the single highest-priority, lowest-cost fix: without it, the several log lines one failed booking produces across bookings/route.ts, email.ts, and the webhook handler have no shared key, so reconstructing what happened to that one booking means grepping by approximate timestamp and hoping nothing else happened in the same second. It remains completely unimplemented in code.
findings.local_evidence: 897 total console.log/error/warn/info calls across app (276 files) and lib (47 files), confirmed by direct grep count this session. grep -rEli 'requestId|request-id|x-request-id|traceparent' across app, lib, and middleware.ts returns exactly 2 hits, both the unrelated `feature_requests.requestId` domain field in app/api/admin/generate-roadmap/route.ts and lib/validations.ts, not a tracing/correlation id.
findings.where_it_should_live: middleware.ts or a new lib/request-id.ts wrapper; rolled out first to the highest-traffic route groups (bookings, payments, the Stripe webhook) per the org's own priority order.
findings.enforcement: checklist for now (no gate can verify 'every log call includes the id' cheaply); a future CI check could flag a console.error call inside app/api/bookings or app/api/stripe that doesn't reference a requestId variable in scope.

findings.title: PostHog error tracking (captureException) never turned on, despite being a config change on an already-paid dependency
findings.principle: Wrap every top-level catch in a route or webhook handler that currently only console.error's on an unexpected (non-business) exception with an additional posthog.captureException(err, { distinctId, ...context }) server-side call (posthog-node is already a dependency), so the same recurring bug groups into one PostHog issue with an occurrence count instead of N disconnected log lines that age out of Netlify's retention window within days.
findings.why: The org's own research (section 5) states this directly: 'Cost: near zero, PostHog is already a paid dependency and already wired client- and server-side; this is a config/adoption change, not new infrastructure. This closes the single biggest and cheapest gap in Solen's observability stack today.' Ten days later it is still at zero adoption. This is explicitly NOT a recommendation to add Sentry: OPS_RUNBOOK.md already records Sentry as a parked owner decision ('email alerting shipped instead'), and that decision should stand; this finding is about turning on a capability inside a tool already paid for and already integrated.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rn captureException app lib --include=*.ts returns 0 hits. posthog-server.ts and posthog-js/posthog-node usage (trackServerEvent) are confirmed present and imported in app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts and elsewhere, so the SDK is live for analytics events but not for error capture.
findings.existing_coverage: none: PostHog is installed and actively used for product analytics (trackServerEvent) but its error-tracking feature specifically has zero call sites.
findings.where_it_should_live: the highest-value catch blocks first: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts, app/api/bookings/route.ts, and any cron route's withCronRun catch in lib/cron-run.ts (one central change point covers all 26 crons at once).
findings.enforcement: checklist / a single change to lib/cron-run.ts's catch block would cover all crons at once; individual route catches need a case-by-case pass.

findings.title: A raw customer email was logged, violating the project's own already-documented PII-in-logs convention
findings.principle: No console.error/console.log/console.warn call interpolates a raw email address, phone number, or full name; log the internal id (user_id, booking_id, salon_id) instead, and look the record up in the access-controlled database when investigating. Enforce with a CI grep: grep -rnE "console\.(error|warn|log)\([^)]*\{[^}]*\b(email|phone)\s*:" app lib must return zero new hits on every PR.
findings.why: This is not a new rule being proposed; it restates one the project already wrote down and then quietly broke. _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md line 33 states as an already-settled fact: 'PII in logs: OTPs no longer logged (2026-07-10 sweep); console.error carries ids not PII by convention, keep it that way.' Without an enforced gate, that convention is only as durable as the next session's memory of a 73-line ops doc.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/admin/tos/notify/route.ts line 85: `console.error("[admin/tos/notify] send failed:", err, { email: user.email });` is a live, current violation.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rnE "console\.(error|warn|log)\([^)]*\{[^}]*\b(email|phone|firstName|lastName|fullName|customerName)\b" app lib --include=*.ts, filtered to metadata-object interpolation specifically (grep -rnE "console\.(error|warn|log)\(.*\{[^}]*\b(email|phone)\s*:" app lib), returned exactly this one hit repo-wide; no CI/lint check currently exists to catch a second one.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the rule is documented in prose (_plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md:33) with no enforcement, hence the live violation.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/admin/tos/notify/route.ts:85 (one-line fix, log user.id instead); a CI grep gate for the standing rule.
findings.enforcement: gate:no-pii-in-logs , the grep pattern above wired as a CI check or PreToolUse hook on app/api and lib edits.

findings.title: The observability research was never frozen into LAW.md; its own Decision-candidates table sits unused
findings.principle: Copy each of observability.md's own 'Decision candidates' table rows (log format, request/trace id, metric framework, SLO source, alert routing, health-check shape, audit trail, PII-in-logs, OpenTelemetry adoption) into _backend-system/LAW.md as a dated, numbered, locked row, in the same one-row-per-axis format _design-system/LOCKFILE.md already uses for frontend decisions, with RATIONALE.md holding the why and QUESTIONS.md holding the one still-open fork (which internal request-id scheme to standardize on).
findings.why: The backend-system folder's own README states its founding reason directly: 'nothing anywhere tells [a fresh session] what to decide. So it decides from training memory.' For observability specifically the research is unusually thorough (22 sources, T1-tagged) and already produced a ready-to-use decision table; the only missing step is the copy-and-date pass that turns 'researched' into 'law.' Until that happens, every new session re-derives (or worse, re-guesses) the same 9 decisions from a 207-line file it may not fully read.
findings.local_evidence: ls _backend-system/*.md returns only README.md; ls _backend-system/audit/ returns 8 files with no observability.md or reliability.md audit. observability.md lines 137-147 already contain a complete 9-row 'Decision candidates' table with a 'recommended for Solen' column, unused outside that file.
findings.absence_proof: Confirmed by direct `ls` of _backend-system/ (only README.md present) and _backend-system/audit/ (8 named files, missing observability and reliability); this matches the orchestrator's own pre-established finding that LAW.md/RATIONALE.md/AUDIT_2026-07-16.md/QUESTIONS.md do not exist anywhere in the folder.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the content that WOULD populate LAW.md already exists verbatim in observability.md's Decision-candidates table; nothing needs to be re-researched, only copied and dated.
findings.enforcement: doc-only; a future PreToolUse-style check could block adding a NEW research/<slug>.md file without a corresponding LAW.md section already existing, mirroring the design-system's own drift gates.

findings.title: No SLI is tracked; the org's own research says this is the actual blocker to picking an honest SLO
findings.principle: Add one more query to the existing daily digest: count of booking-creation attempts that ended in a failed/abandoned/timed-out state (not just 'created' and 'completed') over the same trailing window, expressed as a percentage of total attempts, trended day over day inside the same email. Do NOT build a formal SLO/error-budget policy (release freezes, burn-rate dashboards) on top of it yet; a bare trended percentage is the honest floor at 28 salons, and it is also the prerequisite the org's own research says is missing before a real SLO number can be chosen honestly.
findings.why: observability.md section 3 states plainly: 'right now Solen cannot answer how often does a booking actually fail with a number at all,' and its own recommended path (derive the SLO from what a missed booking actually costs a salon, not an industry benchmark) is blocked without a baseline number to look at first. This is cheap: it is one more query alongside the two the digest already runs, not new infrastructure.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts sections 1-2 (roughly lines 60-92) query bookings CREATED and bookings COMPLETED as raw counts only; no section computes a failure count or a success percentage. grep -rliE 'success.?rate|SLI|SLO' app lib _plans _docs returns exactly one hit, a table-of-contents line in _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md naming the topic, with no implementation behind it.
findings.existing_coverage: none: raw counts exist, a ratio or a failure-side count does not.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts (one more section); the resulting number feeds the SLO-selection conversation in _backend-system/LAW.md once it exists (finding observability-7).
findings.enforcement: checklist (a single new query, easy to verify by reading the digest email once it ships).

findings.title: No per-critical-flow incident runbook and no postmortem discipline exists anywhere
findings.principle: Add a short entry per highest-stakes flow (booking creation, payment capture / webhook processing, payout release) to _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md: the symptom a report would describe, the first three things to check in order (which table, which log scope, which health-probe field), and the safe versus unsafe manual fixes. Separately, after any real incident that reaches the founder (not a routine cron retry the digest already surfaces), write one page within 48 hours -- what happened, the timeline, the root cause, one follow-up action with an owner -- and store it under a new _plans/POSTMORTEMS/ directory. Keep both intentionally short: this is a documentation habit, not a program with a dedicated on-call rotation.
findings.why: _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md is genuinely good at what it covers (monitoring setup, backup/restore steps, cost tracking, open owner decisions) but it answers 'how do I keep the lights on,' not 'a salon says their booking never confirmed, where do I look first' -- the actual question an incident produces. Postmortem discipline is what turns a recurring incident into one fixed root cause instead of a repeated fire-drill; this project's own retro already concluded 'gates work, advice doesn't' for a different domain, and an unwritten postmortem is advice that evaporates by the next incident.
findings.local_evidence: _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md (73 lines, the only file matching *RUNBOOK* in the repo) contains sections for Monitoring, Backups+DR, Data retention, Cost snapshot, Open owner decisions, Security maintenance, and What to add next -- zero symptom-to-diagnosis playbook entries for booking/payment/payout, and zero postmortem template.
findings.absence_proof: find . -iname '*postmortem*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' returns zero files repo-wide; find . -iname '*RUNBOOK*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' returns only _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md; grep -ni 'postmortem\|incident' inside that file returns zero hits (confirmed by reading the full file).
findings.existing_coverage: none for both the per-flow runbook entries and the postmortem template; the daily digest and cron_runs give raw signal but nothing tells a human what to DO with it during a live incident.
findings.where_it_should_live: _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md (new 'Incident playbooks' section, 3 entries); a new _plans/POSTMORTEMS/ directory with a one-page template.
findings.enforcement: checklist / behavioral rule (a postmortem's existence after a real incident can be checked in retro, not gated at commit time).
